To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the PKI family of endogenous PKAc inhibitors are expressed at similar levels in normal and FLC tissues and inhibit DnaJ-PkAc and wtPKAc with similar efficacy.
DnaJ-PkAc has similar activity and inhibition profile to wt-PkAc, suggesting that the endogenous PKI are unlikely to be effective inhibitors in the FLC tumor.
DnaJ-PkAc is inhibited by endogenous PKI inhibitors and that this inhibition is not unique.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of PKI proteins that interact with DnaJ-PkAc and the characterization of these interactions.
the identification of PKI isoforms in the normal liver and FCL tumor and the assessment of their inhibitory properties on DnaJ-PkAc.
the identification of endogenous PKAc inhibitors that can be used to inhibit PKAc in FLC tumors and to identify potential drug targets for the treatment of these tumors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
DnaJ-PkAc is a bona fide PKAc enzyme that can be inhibited by PKI and PKIp-derived peptides, albeit with reduced efficacy compared to wtPKAc.
PKI and DnaJ PKI interactions are similar in both normal liver cells and in FLC tumors.
the PKI isoforms expressed in normal liver and FLP are not likely to encounter DnaJB1-PRKACA fusion protein and therefore do not inhibit DnaJ-PkAc.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the PKI family of endogenous PKAc inhibitors is not perturbed in Dnal-PKAc, and that the PKI-mediated regulation of DnaJPKAc is similar to that of wtPKAc, with the exception that PKI-mediated nuclear export is not observed for DnaJ-PKaC.
PKI and PKA inhibitors are effective at inhibiting DnaJ-PkAc and that PKI and its peptides are effective at inhibitory PKA activity in both normal liver tissue and FLC tumors.
the chimeric enzyme DnaJ-PKA has similar activity to wild type PKA and that it is not inhibited by PKIs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the PKI family of proteins is a potential therapeutic target for inhibiting the oncogenic DnaJ-PkAc kinase.
the PKI inhibitors that are most abundant in the liver and FLC are the PKI isoforms with a high affinity for the PKAc active site, and these are not perturbed in the DnaJ-PkAc enzyme.
PKI isoforms expressed in normal liver and FCLC are capable of inhibiting DnaJ-PkAc, but at levels that may be insufficient to fully suppress the oncogenic activity of this enzyme.
